Phi 1873
Brother Jacobs was born in Detroit, on
November 12, 1853, and died there on
January 30, 1909. His father, Nathaniel
Poole Jacobs, served under President Lin
coln as United States Consul General to
British India. Jacobs, aside from his law
practice and writing, devoted himself to
college affairs. In the field of Greek Letter
Fraternities, in his publication in 1879
of The Greek Letter Societies, he was not
only the pioneer historian, but indubitably
the best qualified authority.
The Phi Chapter, at the time of Jacobs'
initiation, was still in the afterglow of its
successful foundation in 1865. Its early his
tory is recorded in a series of Chronicles,
undertaken annually by undergraduate his
torians. These Chronicles start with the
efforts for a charter in 1854, and continue
through the 70's. Jacobs came immediately
into contact with alumni groups deeply
interested in the success of the new
chap
ter; in Ann Arbor, among others, John M.
Wheeler, Theta '41, James B. Angell,
Sigma '49, Edward S. Dunster, Alpha '56,
James Craig Watson, Phi '57, Charles Ken
dall Adams, Phi '61, George S. Morris,
Zeta '61, Martin L. D'Ooge, Phi '62, Henry

Sherrill, Phi '80, long associates and co
workers with Jacobs in Psi Upsilon.
These groups and their associates estab
lished in Detroit, in 1877, one of the
earliest Alumni Associations of Psi Upsi
lon, whose meeting and annual dinner
continues to be one of the important
events of the Fraternity. Allied to the Phi
Chapter, the Association through the years
has provided leadership for many contri
butions to the University of Michigan, in
cluding the organization, on October 21,
1895, of the University of Michigan
Alumni Association of Detroit, at the call
of Edwin S. Sherrill, Phi '80, which, in
turn, led to the foundation two years later,
in 1897, of the present general Alumni As
sociation of the University of Michigan.
Usually centered at distant points, this
power of fraternal groups to kindle the
flame of general alumni interest and loy
alty, demonstrated often and in many
fields, is a distinct contribution to the
alumni movement, itself one of the pre
eminent characteristics of the American
college system.
In all of this Jacobs took part. These
early contacts stimulated his interest not
only in the history of the chapter, and of
the Fraternity, but in that of his Univer
sity. His services to the Phi were continu
ous throughout his life. First as
Secretary
and then as Treasurer of the Phi corpora
tion. The Hamilton Literary Society, and
its successor. The Psi Upsilon Guild, he
carried on most of the Chapter's philistine
activities. These included the building of

EARL D. BABST
Iota-Phi 1893
Psi Upsilon has been conspicuously for
tunate in the distinguished men who have
been privileged to direct the destinies of
our
Fraternity. As President of the Execu
tive Council from 1924 to 1929, Earl D.
Babst, Iota-Phi '93, held the highest office
of trust and honor which Psi Upsilon can
bestow. One of the country's leading citi
zens, he was the sixth President of the
Council, which was instituted in 1869,
being preceded by William F. Morgan,
Delta '65, Frederic A. Brovra, Lambda '72,
Thomas Thacher, Beta '71, Ward McLean,
Theta '43, and Herbert L. Bridgman,
Gamma '66. His was indeed a difficult
task. While the Fraternity was still recover
ing from the shock of the sudden death of
Herbert L. Bridgman on
September 24,
1924, Brother Babst was elected to suc
ceed the person who for forty-one years
had been our
dearly beloved President, a
veritable "Ark of the Covenant," as he was
affectionately called. His election proved
to be a
surprise to him. In writing to one
of his associates on the Council, Brother
Babst said: "I find myseff somewhat under
the spell of the honor and responsibility
I assumed Tuesday evening! No one had
spoken to me in advance. Naturally, I will
do all I can to meet your expectations and
trust, but shall lean heavily on
you and the
others."
Little did Brother Babst realize when he
stepped down from the Executive Coun
cil's Presidency in 1928 that he would be
still serving as an
honorary member in 1962,
going into his 73rd year in Psi Upsilon.
Born in Cresdine, Ohio, July 6, 1870,
the son of Jacob Babst and Mathilda StoU
Babst, he attended the Kenyon Military
Academy, and entered Kenyon College in
1889. It was there that he joined the Iota
Chapter and became a member of the Fra
ternity which he has long served with dis
tinction and devotion. In his many grace
ful and beauttful addresses at Psi Upsilon

ber of the Phi Chapter.

elected to Phi Beta Kappa. In 1911 the
University of Michigan conferred an hon
orary Master of Arts upon him, and in
1926 Kenyon College bestowed an LL.D.
degree and he received an LL.D. degree
from Michigan University in 1951 and an
LL.D. from Trinity College in 1953.
In 1903 Brother Babst married Alice
Edwina Uhl, the daughter of the late Ed
win F. Uhl, one time Assistant Secretary of
State and Ambassador to Germany. Ad
mitted to the Michigan Bar in 1894, for
eight years he was associated with the
Hon. Otto Kirchner in practice in Detroit.
During this period he was a founder of
the Detroit University School and of the
Detroit University Club, also a director of
the Citizens Savings Bank. From 1902 to
1906 Brother Babst was a member of the
firm of Green, Peters and Babst in Chi
cago, serving as
general counsel of the
National Biscuit Company, of the Ameri
can Radiator Company, and others. In
1906 he moved to New York as general
counsel and later as first Vice-President
of the National Biscuit Company. In 1915
he was elected President of the American
Sugar Refining Company, which office he
held until 1925. During the War, as a
member of the International Sugar Com
mission, he represented the United States
in the alocation of sugar supplies to the
AUies. Since 1925 he has been the chair
man of the board of the American Sugar
Refining Company. He is also a director of
the Chase National Bank and of many
companies.
In spite of his busy career Brother Babst
has always found time to render service
to Kenyon and to Michigan. From 1926 to
1937 he was a trustee of Kenyon College
and Alumni Council. He served on the
Executive Committee of the Alumni Ad
visory Council of the University of Michi
gan from 1907 to 1923. He was President
of the University of Michigan Club of
New York, 1912-1913; President of the
Kenyon Alumni Association of the East,
1915-1917, 1923-1926.
The great Michigan dinner of 1912 in
New York, when Brother Babst was Presi
dent of the New York club launched the
Michigan University Alumni Association,
which was the first state university alumni
association in the country and has con
tinued to be one of the strongest in the
nation.
Through his long and distinguished ca
reer Brother Babst has always been a
loyal
supporter of Psi Upsilon. His invaluable
book, "Occasions in Psi Upsilon," con
taining his addresses at fraternity affairs,
is filled with his devotion to Psi Upsilon,
which to him "has ever been a
fascinating
romance," whfle "at the same time in its
brotherhood it has been a
living reality."
His interest in the activities of the Fra
ternity has ever "been a labor of love,
a
happy labor." His service on the Council
from 1907 to 1929, and life member since
1940, is but typical of the wiUingness of
the prominent and busy leaders in our
nation's life to
accept long tenures of
Council service. Brother Herbert L. Bridgman's forty-seven years of continuous serv
ice on the council was without parallel
in the history of coUege fraternities of
that time. While Brother Babst had an
interlude when he did not serve on coun
cfl that period was covered by his book,
"Occasions in Psi Upsilon" and the writing
and editing of large portions of "The An
nals of Psi Upsilon" as well as the super
vising of its production and his substantial
financial support of this monumental his
tory of our
fraternity.

Jacobs is on familiar ground, for his an

Episcopal minister
in Jackson, Michigan, was a descendent
of Jonathan Edwards. Brother Jacobs'
father, Albert Poole Jacobs, Phi '73, was
a
leading Detroit lawyer, and senior
warden of St. Paul's Cathedral in Detroit.
Unique in fraternity histories is the fact
that the father wrote the first fifty years

completed the history to 1941, in the
Annals of Psi Upsilon. Brother Jacobs has
one sister. Dr. Charlotte B. Newman,
Professor of Bacteriology at Hunter Col

He was selected as a Rhodes Scholar
upon his graduation from the University

named a don, the only American ever to
get a
lecturing fellowship. He stayed in
England for six years as a lecturer in

He joined the Columbia University fac

recognized as an
outstanding teacher be
fore he reached the age of 30, being pro

associate professor in 1929 at the age of
29. He became a full professor in 1936.
His popularity with the faculty was
attested by his election to the presidency
